title: Dutch Defence: the Stonewall, the e5 hole and the e4 fight
outcomes: Names the Stonewall pawns (c6, d5, e6, f5) and the line 1.d4 f5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 e6 4.Nf3 d5 5.O-O Bd6 6.c4 c6 that reaches them, and names the bases of the pawn chains
Finds the one empty square no black pawn can attack (the hole on e5) and plays a sound move for White, and checks whether a black pawn on d6 takes the hole away
Finds a sound move that carries on Black's set-up around e4, and says why the bishop on c8 is the bad bishop and the bishop on d6 the good one
Counts attackers and defenders of e4 before pushing the e-pawn, and recognises a position where White's e5 plan does not apply

steps.text: **Dutch Defence** (ECO A80): 1.d4 f5. Black grabs control of e4 with the first move. In the set-up this lesson follows, Black adds pawns on e6, d5 and c6 to make the **Stonewall**: pawns on c6, d5, e6 and f5. Chains and good and bad bishops are core lessons and are not re-taught here; this lesson asks what this structure gives each side. Step through one main line.

steps.caption: Position after 1.d4 f5, White to move. Step through one main line to the Stonewall; other moves are possible.

line.say: g3 makes room for the bishop on g2.
Nf6 develops the knight; it attacks e4 as well.
Bg2 puts the bishop on the long diagonal.
e6 defends the pawn on f5 and also guards d5.
Nf3 develops the knight and covers e5.
d5 takes the centre and puts a pawn on a light square.
Bd6 puts the dark-squared bishop on a diagonal that reaches g3.
c4 attacks the pawn on d5 and claims space.
c6 defends d5 and completes the Stonewall: pawns on c6, d5, e6 and f5.

steps.text: **Chains have a base (rule of thumb).** In a pawn chain the base is the pawn that defends another pawn and has no pawn defending it. An attack on the base undermines the whole chain; an attack on the head only wins or trades one pawn. Find the bases in the Stonewall.

**White's plan: use e5 (rule of thumb).** With black pawns on c6, d5, e6 and f5, no black pawn attacks e5 now, and none can reach d6 or f6 by moving forward, so e5 is a hole. A knight there cannot be kicked out by a pawn, but a piece can still trade it (for example a bishop on d6). Condition: a black pawn on d6 or f6 takes the hole away. In the next item tap the square that fits.

**Black's plan: the e4 square (rule of thumb).** The pawn on f5 guards e4, so a black knight there is supported by a pawn. In the position after Qc2 the engine rates Ne4 and Qe7 about equally (a few hundredths of a pawn apart at depth 16), but this is one position, not a law. Condition: White has pieces (Nc3, Qc2) that attack e4, so Black needs the supporting pawns. In the next item several moves are sound.

**The price (rule of thumb).** Black's pawns on c6, d5, e6 and f5 stand on light squares, so the bishop on c8 has few moves: the bad bishop. The bishop on d6 is the good one, and the hole on e5 is the other cost of advancing the f-pawn. Tap the squares the bad bishop can reach.

**Count before you push (rule of thumb).** A plan tells you where to look, not whether a move works. White may be tempted to fight for e4 with the e-pawn. Count the pieces and pawns that attack e4 and the ones that defend it. In the next item e4 is tempting; find a better move.

**Both plans depend on the pawns (rule of thumb).** The e5 plan needs a hole, so one black pawn move can remove it. Black's e4 plan needs the f5 pawn and a square White cannot easily attack. Next you predict Ne5 in three positions; they differ by one pawn move each.

steps.title: One pawn move changes whether Ne5 works
steps.prompt: In all three positions White considers Ne5. The first two differ only in Black's sixth move (d5 or d6). The third differs from the first only in Black's last move (h6 instead of a6). Predict each, then check.

steps.text: **What the games show (counts of games, not evaluations).** Masters database: 329,379 games, both players rated 2500 or more. Counts are per position, so other move orders are included. 1.d4 f5: 1,739 games. After 4.Nf3: 4...d5 in 64, 4...Be7 in 52. After 6.c4: 6...O-O in 35, 6...c6 in 29. After 6...c6: 7.b3 in 54, 7.Nc3 in 12, 7.Qc2 in 12 (not all replies are listed). Source: stats.json. Counts do not say which move is better.

**Online counts.** Lichess rated blitz, rapid and classical, September 2026 sample, 4,752,291 games: 24,806 games visit 1.d4 f5. That is 0.22% of games below 900 (394 of 177,947) and 0.72% of games at 2100+ (2,247 of 314,056).
